messages.subject_clean: Deriving density from CL model averaged values
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I might have missed this information somewhere, but any thoughts would be appreciated.

I have fitted 5  conditional likelihood models, including one with an age covariate,  and compared via AICc. The dAICc values are close, so I'm hoping to model average the top models however I'm struggling to find a way to derive my density estimates from the model averaged values. I read on a 2012 forum that this used to be something you were unable to do in secr, so was just wondering if this issue has been cleared up?

Thanks,

Charlotte Patterson

I have a similar problem to Rasmus, with models of different covariates on density all turning out identical (example provided below). Models of these covariates on g0 do not have this problem. Does anyone have any ideas what we might be doing wrong?

Thanks a lot for your help,

Sam

library(secr)

load(url("https://github.com/samual-williams/Hyaena-density/blob/master/inputs.RData?raw=true"))

mD1 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~1, g0~session), mask=maskClosed, detectfn=1, CL=TRUE)

mD2 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~session, g0~session), mask=maskClosed, detectfn=1, CL=TRUE)

mD3 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~LeopardRAI, g0~session), mask=maskClosed, detectfn=1, CL=TRUE)

mD6 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~ReserveSize, g0~session), mask=maskClosed, detectfn=1, CL=TRUE)

mD7 <- secr.fit(cptr_hst, model=list(D~PreyRAI, g0~session), mask=maskClosed, detectfn=1, CL=TRUE)

AIC(mD1, mD2, m3, mD4, mD5, mD6, mD7)

Hi Sam,

Are these mask covariates?  I'm thinking that the fitting function is looking for this covariates in the mask and not finding them?

For session covs, from the multi-session vignette:
"Other variation among sessions may be modelled with session-specific covariates. These are provided to secr.fit on-the-fly in the argument ‘sessioncov’ (they cannot be embedded in the capthist object like detector or individual covariates). The value for ‘sessioncov’ should be a dataframe with one row per session. Each column is a potential predictor in a model formula; other columns are ignored."

Can't model variation in density using trap covariates  if that what these relative abundance indices correspond to. Density is a point process across the mask--maybe it varies spatially across the mask, or it changes across sessions, or both.

If CL=TRUE, you can't model variation in density at all. The point process is conditioned out of the likelihood--density is a derived parameter.

Cheers,

John

messages.body_plain:
A constant-a0 model assumes a constant relationship between a0 and the underlying parameter a, across the units (sessions?) in which a0 is held constant. This breaks down if the detector array or usage or number of occasions vary, as each of these affects a independently of a0. So I think you were right, but it depends a little on how you were using it (the units across which a0 held constant).
Sorry for delay.

I am trying to fit a model, in which sigma and density can vary according to a two-class habitat covariate (which I already included into the habitatmask, called ‘Community’). fn2 <- function (xy1, xy2, mask) {

if (missing(xy1)) return("noneuc")

xy1 <- addCovariates(xy1, mask)

xy2 <- addCovariates(xy2, mask)

sig1 <- as.numeric(covariates(xy1)$noneuc) # sigma(x,y) at detectors

euc <- edist(xy1, xy2)

sig <- outer (sig1, sig2, FUN = function(s1, s2) (s1 + s2)/2)

euc / sig

}

fit.HN_e2_DHab_SigHab <- secr.fit(MRCH_e2, model = list(D~ Community,  noneuc ~ Community), mask=clippedmask_e2_cov, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE, details = list(autoini = 2, knownmarks = FALSE, userdist = fn2), fixed = list(sigma = 1))

Hi Murray,

We recently conducted a session without a single detection. I would like to know, given the sampling effort, how confident I can be that not as single individual was present in the study site during the survey :-)

Based on the suggestion of Jose Jimenez on Researchgate, I started to run multisession secr analysis including one session that does not contain a single detection. The idea is to use the information from the site without any detection (sites and usage), and the capture histories from the other sites with positives results to compute the SE and lower and upper confidence interval of the density estimate for the site without detections. I plan to use sessions with positive results conducted in similar habitats and with similar topographical features, as habitat and topographical features could affect detection probability.

So far I used session as session factor on Density and run following model: M0 <-secr.fit(capthist_NWA_VSN, mask=list(mask_13_NWA,mask_13_VSN), model = list(D~session, g0~1, sigma~1),verify=TRUE)

Does it make sense and if yes, how many sessions with positive results would be needed to get a good approximation of SE and lower and upper confidence interval for the site without a single detection?

I noticed that sometimes the variance calculation failed.

Many thanks in advance

Best wishes

Fridolin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Fridolin,

I’ve run a (basic) analysis like this before to estimate density where individuals were reasonably expected to exist but none were captured. As you propose, it calculates a (low) density with standard error  https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/drds352entire.pdf

If you are in the converse situation, where you want to reasonably confirm expected absence, you would also need to set some reasonable subjective expectation of what constitutes absence, as SECR will always give some positive (but small) value of density for the upper bound, if not also point, estimate.

Based on SECR we implement a framework for this called Rapid Eradication Assessment, which is used to confirm the absence of pests on islands following eradication and a series of non-detections. The original methods paper is here:  https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.12147 and further simulations here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.12753 and we have a forthcoming paper in review with further extensions which are implemented in a beta form here:  www.rea.is <http://www.rea.is> (i.e. still a bit buggy).

I am happy to provide R code. There is still always more work to do developing the REA method. In particular the underlying population growth model is simplistic (unbounded exponential) and so the REA is only really suitable when you are expecting to detect <10 individuals if any (recall you are really expecting none). We’re currently working on a different tool to estimate number of pest management survivors when >0 but still low (and unmarked cues).

Regards,

   James

If there are no detections at one site (and on the other grids, the populations are relatively detectable), I would imagine the gradient for the likelihood of log(D_sessionwithoutdetections) looks pretty flat: the likelihood for log(D) = -15 vs. -20, vs. -30 might be nearly exactly the same.You might be able to get a usable derived estimate of D if you fit the multi-session model using  the conditional likelihood? John

valid.userdist <- function (userdist, detector, xy1, xy2, mask, sessnum) {
    if (is.null(userdist)) {
        ## default to Euclidean distance
        result <- edist(xy1, xy2)
    }
    else {
        if (any(detector %in% .localstuff$polydetectors)) {
            stop ("userdist cannot be used with polygon detector types;")
        }
        if (is.function(userdist))
        {
            OK <- getuserdistnames(userdist) %in% names(covariates(mask))
            if ((length(OK)>0) & !all(OK))
                stop ("covariates required by userdist function not in mask : ",
                      paste(getuserdistnames(userdist)[!OK], collapse=','))
            result <- do.call(userdist, c(list(xy1, xy2, mask)))
        }
        else {
            if (is.character(userdist)) {
                userdist <- get(userdist, pos=-1)
            }

            if (is.list(userdist) & !is.data.frame(userdist)) {
                if (missing(sessnum))
                    stop("This use does not yet allow for session-specific userdist")
                else
                    result <- userdist[[sessnum]]
            }
            else {
                result <- userdist
            }
        }
        if (!all(dim(result) == c(nrow(xy1), nrow(xy2))))
            stop ("invalid distance matrix dim = ", dim(result)[1], ',', dim(result)[2])
        baddist <- (!is.finite(result)) | (result<0) | is.na(result)
        if (any(baddist)) {
            warning ("replacing infinite, negative and NA userdist values with 1e10")
            result[baddist] <- 1e10
        }
    }
    result
}
